newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK policemen loyal to queen resist new allegiance.
newsitem.headline: HK policemen loyal to queen resist new allegiance.

text.p: A group of Hong Kong Chinese police officers said on Thursday they refused to give up their loyalty to Britain's Queen Elizabeth and demanded a retirement package rather than serve under Chinese rule.
The group of eight feared the future government might give orders that ran against their conscience, their leader said.

Senior inspector Chik Ki-wai said the eight, who all hold British passports, wanted to take early retirement ahead of the territory's handover to Beijing next Monday night, just as expatriate collegues had been allowed to do.
But he said their request had been turned down because of their Chinese ethnicity.

Chik, a veteran of 21 years' service, told a news conference the dispute was mostly about the right to work where they wanted -- they had joined the Royal Hong Kong police force and sworn an oath to the Queen, and did not want to serve a new government.
He said the eight were afraid of what they may face as law enforcers after the flag change.

"We do not want to be in that position in the future," he said. "That's why we take the painful and difficult decision to leave the service now and not to be faced with any act or any order given to us which might be contrary to (our) conscience."
Chik said he did not want to criticise the future government. He stressed police morale was good and that he did not expect other officers to follow the group.
But he said he and his seven colleagues had been shocked and frightened when the colonial administration said it would hand their retirement request over to the post-handover government.
They would refuse to return to duty on July 1, he said, even though they faced being charged with desertion.
A police spokesman said the eight had been refused early retirement because they did not qualify under the rules.
"If they still want to leave the force by way of resignation before June 30, 1997, the Commissioner of Police is prepared to consider waiving the required period of notice," he said.
Chik acknowledged the eight could simply resign.
But he said they were outraged the government refused to give them the same early retirement deal that expatriates got, even though they were all British citizens.

"If you are told your company will be taken over by another company with which you may take a different personal or political stance, and you are told you can quit but your expat colleagues were given the option to retire with full benefits, would you resign or would you fight for your rights?"
